w: Completed in 1991 near the University of Arizona, this single-minaret, single-dome mosque serves as prayer space and community hub for Muslims across southern Arizona. It holds all five daily prayers plus Friday Jumu'ah, drawing a congregation that reaches well beyond the city itself.
s: A single minaret serving all of southern Arizona
_facts: completed 1991
located near the University of Arizona
single minaret and dome
serves Muslims across southern Arizona, holds daily prayers and Jumu'ah

w: The city's name comes from this peak: 'Tucson' derives from O'odham Cuk Son, 'the base is black,' describing the basalt where the valley's first farmers worked the Santa Cruz River. In the 1910s, university students hauled basalt up its east face to build a 160-foot block letter 'A,' earning the nickname 'A' Mountain.
s: The peak that gave Tucson its name and its giant A
_facts: name 'Tucson' derives from O'odham Cuk Son, meaning the base is black
site of the valley's first farming along the Santa Cruz River
160-ft basalt block letter A built by students in the 1910s
also known as 'A' Mountain, part of a 272-acre park

w: Founded in 1893 by authority of the Arizona Territorial Legislature -- nearly two decades before statehood -- this was originally built to collect and protect archaeological finds. It's now the state's museum of anthropology, exhibiting and researching artifacts from the region on the University of Arizona campus.
s: A territorial-era museum of archaeology, pre-statehood
_facts: founded 1893 by the Arizona Territorial Legislature
originally a repository for archaeological resources
operated by the University of Arizona
focuses on exhibition, education and research

w: Founded in 1692 by Jesuit missionary Eusebio Kino, the original church was demolished in an Apache raid in 1770 and rebuilt between 1783 and 1797 using O'odham labor -- the oldest European structure in Arizona. Some 200,000 visit yearly, many arriving on foot or horseback, still known locally as Wa:k, 'water place.'
s: Arizona's oldest European building, still a pilgrim site
_facts: founded 1692 by Eusebio Kino
original church destroyed in an Apache raid, 1770
rebuilt 1783-1797, oldest European structure in Arizona
draws ~200,000 visitors a year, known as Wa:k in O'odham

w: A 49-acre botanical garden and nature preserve in Casas Adobes, its name borrowed from Tohono O'odham words for 'desert corner.' Thirty-eight bird species live here year-round, another 57 pass through seasonally, alongside Gila monsters and bobcats -- named a great botanical garden of the world by Travel+Leisure, 2008.
s: A 'desert corner' with 95 bird species passing through
_facts: 49-acre site in Casas Adobes
name means 'desert corner' in O'odham
38 resident bird species plus 57 seasonal migrants
named a Great Botanical Garden of the World, Travel+Leisure 2008

w: Announced in 2012 by church president Thomas S. Monson, this LDS temple in the Catalina Foothills broke from convention with an Art Deco design by FFKR Architects -- unusual for a Latter-day Saint temple. Its dome, topped with a statue of the angel Moroni, crowns a 38,216-square-foot building on a 7.4-acre site.
s: An Art Deco Mormon temple in the Catalina Foothills
